cim: Editorial: The potential peril of AI is tremendous. So is the potential promise.
cim_eredeti: Editorial: The potential peril of AI is tremendous. So is the potential promise.
szoveg_eredeti:
Editorials represent the institutional view of the newspaper. They are written and edited by the editorial staff, which operates separately from the news department. Editorial writers are not involved in newsroom operations.

The Gibbes Museum of Art in Charleston has operated 3D exhibits for visitors with limited vision. A new AI-assisted app could further enliven that experience.

Most of the conversation lately about artificial intelligence has been negative — from new college grads worried about their future employment to Anthropic co-founder and CEO Dario Amodei and other AI creators worried about its potential to quite literally destroy humanity.

There’s good reason for concern. This is the most powerful technology humans have ever created, and the federal government has refused to even consider putting any sort of restrictions on its development and use — has refused, even, to require public disclosure about its use — and has kept in place laws that make it nearly impossible for its current masters to coordinate their own restrictions.

We’ll only hear more of the downside now that Democrats are taking control of the Congress in part by pointing to the dangers of AI, and the deceit that goes into propping up ever more data centers, and the money being made by people playing a role in the hands-off government policies.

To those long-awaited regulations, we say bring ’em on. Carefully. With an understanding of both the real threat if China or other potential enemies get out ahead of us, and also of the vast good that artificial intelligence can do if it’s designed to … do good. The examples are all around us.

This summer, Saif Chaundry, an honors student at the College of Charleston, started working on a phone application that uses AI tools to generate spoken narration for the visually impaired. The project was inspired by the college’s grant-funded Summer Undergraduate with Faculty project.

The smartphone app captures video stream, sends it to a locally hosted AI model on a PC, removing the potential need for data center involvement. Within seconds, a description of the scene is generated with AI assistance and spoken aloud by the smart device. The application can identify nearby pedestrians, vehicles, buildings, nature and so forth, communicating this information to the user. In addition to real-time capture, the application allows users to upload prerecorded footage of other locations that can be described to them.

“I wanted to work on this project because it is computationally difficult yet can still have an impact on someone’s daily life,” Mr. Chaundry, a first-generation college student, told the College Today.

For blind residents in Charleston, this means a safer trip through busy crosswalks crowded with college students carelessly talking on their phones. The same app could also describe the beauty of Brookgreen Gardens to someone who has never been there. Or the inside of the Gibbes Museum of Art, which has previously operated 3D exhibits for visitors with limited vision. The app could make our state's county parks and walking trails more accessible to residents who have not had the opportunity to explore them. The potential here is endless.

It’s far from the first effort to use AI to break down personal barriers. AI tools have been used by neurodivergent professionals to transcribe their work emails, map out daily schedules and offer focus on cognitively challenging tasks. Seeing AI, a similar app, can read out complex texts and identify paper money aloud to the visually impaired. Voice commands can assist users with mobility impairments, and speech-to-text apps can be used to draft pitches and reports by workers unable to use a keyboard.

And there's no telling where AI tools could take us to further break down those barriers. But we'll never know if we go overboard in our efforts to correct the absence of any meaningful government regulations.

This isn't to say that artificial intelligence should go unrestricted. To the contrary; these positive applications of AI would benefit from protections against the bad actors who've already abused its potential for their own gain.

Beyond the existential threats that might or might not be overblown, there are the more mundane threats that are with us here and now. Cybercriminals and scammers have abused deepfake software to scam South Carolina residents out of millions of dollars. In 2025, the Internet Crime Complaint Center received more than 22,000 complaints reporting AI-related crimes, adding up to $893 million.

To the extent that humans still have the capacity to control artificial intelligence, we need to do so: for instance, putting limits on how it can be used in our schools, by law enforcement and in government in general, and requiring disclosure of all uses, and making it clear that either its creators or its users (or both) are criminally and civilly liable when it does harm.

We need restrictions, as well, to protect everyone's personal online security and privacy. Barriers must be put in place to make sure that those fears that have taken over our imagination aren't realized, and that the tools developed are made for humanity’s enrichment, not its demise.

But while public policy makers decide what sort of constraints we need on AI, let's not forget the potential good it could provide if we manage to get that regulation right.
